title: Event Loop & Coroutines
summary: How single-threaded cooperative concurrency works in Python: coroutines and async/await, the event loop, asyncio.run, the three kinds of awaitable, and how await hands control back to the loop.

blocks.text: A web server spends most of its life **waiting**: for a database to answer, for a client to send the next byte, for an API on the other side of the world. `asyncio` lets one Python thread keep thousands of those waits in flight at once, by switching to other work every time it would otherwise sit idle.

By the end of this chapter you can explain the difference between ==concurrency== and ==parallelism==, write and run coroutines with `async def` and `await`, describe what the event loop does in one turn, start a program with `asyncio.run`, and predict exactly where your code switches from one task to another.

blocks.title: Before you start
blocks.text: You need Python 3.11 or newer for every example here. Run them as files (`python demo.py`), not in Jupyter: notebooks already run a loop, and `asyncio.run` refuses to start a second one.

**Concurrency** means several tasks are in progress at the same time, their lifetimes overlapping. **Parallelism** means several tasks are executing at the same instant, on several CPU cores. A chef with three pans on the stove is concurrent; three chefs are parallel.

`asyncio` gives you concurrency only. One thread runs one piece of Python at a time, and it switches between tasks *cooperatively*: a task keeps running until it reaches an `await` that has to wait, and only then does another task get a turn.
All three run work concurrently, but they switch at different moments and cost very different amounts of memory. The deciding question is usually *what are my tasks waiting on*.

blocks.title: The 10,000 connections test
blocks.text: 10,000 threads need gigabytes of stack before they do anything. 10,000 coroutines fit in about 20 MB, which is why asyncio servers can hold that many idle connections on a small machine.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Reaching for asyncio to speed up number crunching. A coroutine that computes for two seconds blocks every other coroutine for those two seconds; asyncio only helps when tasks spend their time waiting.

pages.title: Calling a coroutine function does not run it

blocks.text: `async def` defines a **coroutine function**. Calling it does not execute the body: it returns a **coroutine object**, a paused computation that runs only when something awaits it or wraps it in a Task.

lines: await asyncio.sleep(1)   # pretend this is a network call
result = await coro      # now the body runs
blocks.note: the body of fetch() starts only at `await coro`

blocks.text: `await` suspends the current coroutine until the awaited one finishes, then evaluates to its return value, or re-raises its exception exactly as a normal call would.

blocks.title: Forgetting await
blocks.text: `fetch()` on its own creates a coroutine and throws it away. Python warns `RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'fetch' was never awaited` and the body never runs.

blocks.title: Awaiting a plain function
blocks.text: `await time.sleep(1)` fails with `TypeError: object NoneType can't be used in 'await' expression`, after already blocking the whole loop for a second. Use `await asyncio.sleep(1)`.

pages.title: Under the hood: a generator in disguise

blocks.text: Coroutines are built on generators. Advancing one is a `send(None)`: it runs to the next point where it must wait and stops there. When it finishes, `StopIteration.value` carries its return value. The loop never calls your code directly; a Task does these sends for it.

blocks.text: The event loop is a scheduler with three lists: callbacks that are **ready** to run, **timers** waiting for their time, and **file descriptors** being watched for I/O. Every turn does the same four things.

blocks.q: What does calling `fetch()` return if `fetch` is defined with `async def`?
a_bullets: A coroutine object; the body has not run yet
It runs only when awaited or wrapped in a Task

blocks.q: Two tasks each print 0, 1, 2 with `await asyncio.sleep(0)` after every print. What is the output?
a_bullets: `sleep(0)` suspends, so the other ready task gets a turn each time

blocks.q: Your service hashes large files in a coroutine and other requests time out. Why?
a_bullets: Hashing is CPU work with no await that suspends
It blocks the single thread; move it to a process pool

items: asyncio is **concurrency** on one thread, never parallelism
Switches happen only at an `await` that actually waits
Calling a coroutine function returns a coroutine object; `await` runs it
The loop runs ready callbacks, waits for I/O or timers, and repeats
Use it for network-bound work; use processes for CPU-bound work
